newsitem.title: UK: Gulf battle for Clyde enters final hours.
newsitem.headline: Gulf battle for Clyde enters final hours.

text.p: The bitter bid battle for Clyde Petroleum entered its final hours on Tuesday with Gulf Canada Resources agonisingly close to the 50 percent needed to secure victory but the outcome still far from certain.

Gulf Canada said on Monday it had shares or acceptances amounting to 40.97 percent of Clyde, but Clyde shares remained under Gulf's offer price of 120 pence per share -- which values the company at 494 million pounds ($800 million) -- as dealers said the outcome was balanced on a knife-edge.
Clyde shares were down 1p at 115-1/2p ahead of the 1300 GMT deadline for acceptances, with a paltry 126,574 shares traded.
"Obviously it (the bid) could go either way, but with the amount of shares Gulf are sitting on I'd be surprised if they didn't get it," said one dealer.
Industry analysts were similarly cautious. "With just hours to go I have no strong gut feeling one way or the other. It's just too close to call," said one who declined to be named.
One of Clyde's major shareholders, PDFM, has already tendered its 14.9 percent stake at the 120 pence per share offer, but other institutional investors' intentions were not clear.
PDFM and other investors sold in the open market, leaving Gulf Canada with 29.9 percent of Clyde, the maximum level a bidder is allowed to buy in the market under British rules.

There has been widespread speculation that Schroders Plc, Clyde's largest shareholder with a 19.5 percent stake, would stick with the takeover target, but a source at the fund manager declined to comment on its stance on Tuesday morning.

Gulf's original offer for Clyde was pitched at 105 pence per share but raised after fiery exchanges on the value of the exploration and production firm's assets and a sceptical reaction to the original offer by analysts and shareholders alike.
Gulf's attempts to woo investors with its higher offer suddenly made strong progress earlier last week as crude oil prices weakened.
Analysts are divided on the wisdom of accepting the Gulf offer, with some saying that it is better to accept Gulf Canada's cash rather than see Clyde's share price slip if the bid fails.
The E&P sector has already been one of the best performing on the London stock exchange after being fuelled by takeover bid hopes following a flurry of acquisitions since late 1995.
Together with a flow of positive announcements on new oil finds, the sector has continued its bull run so far this year and many pundits see further gains ahead.
